Every language region has its own way of life, and that sometimes creates misunderstanding between the regions. Foreigners who sign a work contract in Switzerland must first get used to the respective language regime of the region.

Sometimes German needs a subject even though there is no real subject. German inserts "es" — a placeholder with NO meaning of its own.
Kabhi German ko subject chahiye hota hai jab koi asli subject nahi hota. German "es" daalta hai — ek placeholder jiska koi matlab nahi.
Weather expressions almost always require formal "es".

The infinitive or dass-clause is the real content; "es" only holds the subject position until it arrives.

Strictly speaking this use has its own name — Korrelat-es — because a real clause does follow, and the "es" vanishes if that clause moves to the front. Chapter 5 covers it in full. The weather, time and es gibt cases above are different: there no clause ever follows, so the "es" can never disappear.

Weather, time aur es gibt wale cases isse alag hain, kyunki wahan koi clause aati hi nahi, isliye wahan "es" kabhi gayab nahi hota.

Sometimes German places es before a clause simply to announce that important information is coming: Es freut mich, dass du gekommen bist. The real content is the clause — not "es". Move the clause to first position, and this "es" disappears: Dass du gekommen bist, freut mich.

Sometimes German places "es" before a subordinate or infinitive clause. This "es" does not have its own meaning — it simply announces the important information that comes later.
Es freut mich, dass du gekommen bist.
Kabhi German subordinate ya infinitive clause se pehle "es" rakh deta hai. Iska apna koi matlab nahi hota — yeh sirf pehle se signal de deta hai ki asli baat aage aa rahi hai.

Every verb needs certain information to form a complete sentence. Without it, the sentence feels incomplete.
Har verb ko ek poore sentence banane ke liye kuch jaankaari chahiye hoti hai. Uske bina, sentence adhoora lagta hai.
Ergänzung is REQUIRED — without it the sentence is incomplete. Angabe is OPTIONAL extra information — the sentence still works without it.
Ergänzung REQUIRED hota hai — uske bina sentence adhoora hota hai. Angabe OPTIONAL extra jaankaari hota hai — uske bina bhi sentence chalta hai.
Complements come in several types depending on the verb.
Complements verb ke hisaab se kai types mein aate hain.
A simple method: find the verb, ask a question (Who? What? Whom? To whom? For what? About what?), then apply the removal test.
1. Find the verb. 2. Ask Who?/What?/Whom?/To whom?/For what?/About what? 3. Required answer = Ergänzung. Optional answer = Angabe.

Tarika simple hai. Pehle verb dhoondo, phir uske hisaab se sawaal poochho — Kaun? Kya? Kisko? Kiske liye? Kis baare mein? — aur uske baad removal test lagao: us shabd ko hata kar dekho, sentence chalta hai ya toot jaata hai.
These common B2 verbs have fixed prepositional or case complements — memorize them as pairs.
In common B2 verbs ka apna fixed preposition ya case hota hai. Inhe jodi ki tarah yaad karo — verb akela yaad karne se sentence banate waqt case galat ho jaata hai.
Some verbs need only a subject; others need two or more complements at once.
Ich kaufe meiner Schwester ein Buch.
Kuch verbs ko sirf subject chahiye hota hai; doosron ko ek saath do ya zyaada complements chahiye hote hain.
Every German verb has its own fixed "pattern" of complements. The next chapter (Valenz von Verben) studies this pattern in detail.
Har German verb ka apna fixed complements ka "pattern" hota hai. Agla chapter (Valenz von Verben) is pattern ko detail mein padhta hai.
These mistakes come from dropping a required preposition, or using the wrong case for a fixed complement.
"warten" needs the preposition "auf" + Akkusativ — it cannot take a direct object alone.
"sich interessieren für" is reflexive and needs the preposition "für" + Akkusativ.
"brauchen" requires an Akkusativ object — the sentence is incomplete without it.
Yeh galtiyaan required preposition chhod dene se, ya fixed complement ke liye galat case use karne se hoti hain.

A third group sits in between: über-, unter-, um-, durch-, wider- can go either way. Stress on the prefix → it separates, and the meaning is literal (Ich ziehe um = I move house). Stress on the stem → it stays attached, and the meaning is figurative (Ich übertrage die Daten = I transfer the data). This is why umziehen splits but übertragen does not.

Conflicts in the team often arise because someone simply accepts a problem. A colleague should instead listen closely and respond with an I-message. Whoever takes on an argument, instead of avoiding it, usually resolves the conflict faster. Some managers therefore propose a short conversation as soon as tension lingers in the team. This way, the whole team's ability to concentrate can quickly be restored. Whoever addresses conflicts openly, instead of ignoring them, ends up taking on more responsibility.

The position of nicht depends on what you're negating. Deny the WHOLE statement (Satznegation) and "nicht" goes late: Ich arbeite heute nicht. Deny just ONE part (Sondernegation) and "nicht" goes directly before it, usually followed by "sondern": Ich arbeite nicht heute, sondern morgen.

You are a warm, encouraging German (B2) tutor for a Hindi/English-speaking learner. The lesson is STELLUNG VON NICHT — SATZ- VS. SONDERNEGATION (B2 level): the position of "nicht" depends entirely on what is being negated. Satznegation (whole-sentence negation) places "nicht" as late as possible, usually just before the second verb or the right sentence bracket (Ich arbeite heute nicht. / Anna hat den Film nicht gesehen.). Sondernegation (special/partial negation) places "nicht" directly before the ONE element being negated, often followed by "sondern" (Nicht Anna kommt, sondern Rohan. / Ich fahre nicht heute, sondern morgen.). The SAME sentence with "nicht" in a different position can mean something completely different. Do NOT expect kein vs nicht distinctions (already taught earlier), double negation, Litotes, or nuanced negation words (kaum, keineswegs, keinesfalls) — those are out of scope; do not flag their absence. The position of "nicht" depends on the question: "What do you want to negate?" There are two possibilities: the WHOLE sentence, or just ONE part.
"nicht" kahaan rakhna hai, yeh ek hi baat par depend karta hai — tum kya negate karna chahte ho. Do hi options hain: poora sentence, ya sirf ek hissa. Isliye position sochne se pehle yeh decide karo.
If the entire statement is negative, place "nicht" as late as possible — usually before the second verb or the right sentence bracket.
Anna hat den Film nicht gesehen.
Agar poori baat negative hai, to "nicht" ko sentence mein jitna aage ho sake rakho — aksar woh doosre verb ya right bracket ke theek pehle baithta hai.
Only ONE element is negated. "nicht" comes directly before that element, usually followed by "sondern".
Ich fahre nicht heute, sondern morgen.
Wir wohnen nicht in Berlin, sondern in Hamburg.
Yahan sirf ek hissa negate hota hai. Aise case mein "nicht" us hisse ke seedhe pehle aata hai, aur aksar uske baad "sondern" se sahi baat batayi jaati hai.

In Perfekt and with modal verbs, "nicht" sits inside the sentence bracket, just before the final verb element.
Anna hat das Buch nicht gelesen.
Perfekt aur modal verbs ke saath "nicht" bracket ke andar rehta hai, matlab aakhri verb se theek pehle. Uske baad kuch nahi aata.
"nicht" works the same way inside subordinate clauses — placed relative to what it negates.

Standard German avoids double negation — one negative (nichts, niemand, nie, kein) is always enough. But Litotes deliberately pairs "nicht" with a negative-leaning word on purpose — nicht schlecht (quite good), nicht unmöglich (possible) — to sound softer and more diplomatic.

In Standard German one negative word does the whole job. Adding a second one does not make the sentence “more negative” — it just makes it ungrammatical. (English dialects allow “I don’t know nothing”; German never does.) The one exception is deliberate, stylistic Litotes, which this chapter covers below.

Standard German mein ek negative word hi poora kaam kar deta hai. Doosra jodne se sentence zyada negative nahi banta — bas galat ho jaata hai. English ki kuch dialects mein "I don’t know nothing" chalta hai, par German mein kabhi nahi. Ek hi exception hai, aur woh jaan-boojhkar kiya jaata hai — Litotes, jo aage aa raha hai.
One negative word is normally enough — never add a second one.
Ek negative word normally kaafi hota hai — doosra jodne ki zaroorat nahi padti.

The lesson is NUANCIERTE NEGATION (B2 level): German offers a scale of negation strengths, not just neutral "nicht"/"kein". Weak (spoken register): kaum (hardly), kaum noch (hardly any longer), nicht besonders (not particularly), nicht wirklich (not really). Partial/softening: nicht unbedingt (not necessarily), nicht gerade (not exactly), längst nicht (far from — medium/formal). Strong (formal register): keineswegs (by no means), keinesfalls (under no circumstances), durchaus nicht (definitely not). These expressions differ not just in strength but also in register (spoken vs formal). Do NOT expect irony, sarcasm, C1 rhetorical devices, or dialectal negation forms — those are out of scope; do not flag their absence. The learner wrote the text below. Read the scale from the mildest to the most emphatic. Two different things are happening on it: nicht wirklich, nicht besonders and kaum are PARTIAL — a little bit is still true (Ich kenne ihn kaum means you do know him slightly). nicht is the plain, COMPLETE negation. And längst nicht, durchaus nicht, keineswegs, keinesfalls are complete negations with extra emphasis added.
nicht wirklich → nicht besonders → kaum → nicht → längst nicht → durchaus nicht → keineswegs → keinesfalls

Scale ko halke se sabse strong tak padho. Yahan do alag cheezein ho rahi hain. nicht wirklich, nicht besonders aur kaum partial hote hain — matlab thoda bahut sach rehta hai (Ich kenne ihn kaum ka matlab hai ki thoda toh jaante ho). nicht seedha aur poora negation hai. Aur längst nicht, durchaus nicht, keineswegs, keinesfalls poora negation hain, bas usme extra zor lag jaata hai.
Choose the right register — spoken expressions in casual conversation, formal ones in writing and presentations.
keineswegs, keinesfalls, durchaus nicht, längst nicht
Register ka dhyaan rakho — casual baat mein spoken wale expressions, aur writing ya presentation mein formal wale.
The same base statement changes meaning dramatically depending on which negation you choose.
Base sentence wahi hai, bas negation badal rahi hai — aur matlab kaafi badal jaata hai. Isliye sirf "nicht" par atakna nahi chahiye.
These mistakes come from stacking a nuanced expression with an extra "nicht", or picking the wrong strength for the intended meaning.
"kaum" is already a complete negation-like expression — never add "nicht" alongside it.
"keinesfalls" alone carries the full negative force — a second "nicht" is redundant and wrong.
"kaum" already carries the near-negative meaning, so it can never be combined with "kein" — that makes the sentence ungrammatical.
"keineswegs" already means "by no means" — do not add a separate "nicht" before it.
Because "kaum" is already near-negative, it pairs with "etwas", not "nichts" — "kaum nichts" is a double negative.

Yeh galtiyan aksar isliye hoti hain ki jo expression khud hi negative hai, uske saath ek aur negative jod diya jaata hai. Ek baat clear rakho — Ich bin keineswegs müde galat nahi hai, woh bas strong negation hai.

The verb must go to the END of the obgleich-clause, not stay in second position.
Subject "es" must come before the verb-end position — the whole clause needs verb-final word order.

After the obgleich-clause the main clause must start with its verb (geht er) — "aber" cannot occupy that slot. In formal writing a second concession word is also redundant, since "obgleich" already carries it. "obgleich" introduces a Nebensatz — the verb goes to the very end.
Which register is "obgleich" typically used in?
"obgleich" is common in reports, newspapers, and formal writing.
Obgleich er krank ist, geht er zur Arbeit.
Obgleich er krank ist, aber geht er arbeiten.
Wir fahren nach Berlin, obgleich das Wetter schlecht ist.
Never combine "obgleich" with "aber" — the concession is already expressed by "obgleich" alone.
Which conjunction is more common in spoken German?
"obwohl" is the everyday, spoken equivalent; "obgleich" is the formal, written one.
"obgleich" means exactly what "obwohl" means — although — with the same verb-end Nebensatz word order.
The only real difference is register: "obgleich" belongs in reports, newspapers, and formal writing; "obwohl" belongs in everyday speech.

sodass and infolgedessen both mean the same thing — "as a result" — but they work completely differently. sodass introduces a subordinate clause with the verb at the END, inside ONE sentence. Infolgedessen starts a brand-new independent sentence, with the verb in Position 2.

A consequence sentence answers: what happened as a result? Cause leads to consequence.
Es regnete stark, sodass wir zu Hause blieben.
Consequence sentence yeh batata hai ki kisi baat ka result kya nikla. Pehle cause aata hai, phir uska result.
"sodass" means "so that / as a result / with the result that." It introduces a subordinate clause — the verb goes to the END.
Anna war krank, sodass sie nicht zur Arbeit ging.
Es schneite stark, sodass der Verkehr stillstand.
Rohan lernte viel, sodass er die Prüfung bestand.

"sodass" ka matlab hai "jiske result mein" ya "isliye". Dhyaan rakho ki yeh result batata hai, purpose nahi — purpose ke liye damit aata hai. "sodass" ek subordinate clause banata hai, isliye verb sentence ke end mein chala jaata hai.
The main clause comes first, then a comma, then "sodass" + subordinate clause with verb-final order.
Pehle main clause aata hai, phir comma, aur uske baad "sodass" wala clause — jiska verb sentence ke end mein jaata hai.
"infolgedessen" means "as a consequence / consequently / as a result." It is a Konjunktionaladverb — it STARTS A NEW independent sentence, with the verb in Position 2.
Es regnete stark. Infolgedessen blieben wir zu Hause.
Die Maschine war defekt. Infolgedessen musste die Produktion gestoppt werden.
"infolgedessen" ka matlab hai "iske result mein" ya "isliye". Yeh Konjunktionaladverb hai, matlab yeh ek naya poora sentence shuru karta hai — aur uske turant baad verb aata hai, Position 2 par.
Compare the two structures directly — subordinate clause versus independent sentence.
Es war kalt, sodass wir drinnen blieben.
Es war kalt. Infolgedessen blieben wir drinnen.
Dono ko saath rakh kar dekho. sodass ek hi sentence ke andar subordinate clause banata hai, aur infolgedessen ek alag naya sentence shuru karta hai. Yahi asli fark hai.
Never confuse the direction of the logic — weil gives the reason, sodass gives the result.
Ich blieb zu Hause, weil ich krank war.
Ich war krank, sodass ich zu Hause blieb.
Direction ka dhyaan rakho — weil batata hai ki kyun hua, aur sodass batata hai ki uske baad kya hua. Dono ek hi baat ko ulti taraf se kehte hain.
"infolgedessen" is very common in reports, newspapers, business German, and scientific writing. "sodass" works in both speaking and writing.
These mistakes come from mixing up sentence boundaries and word order between the two structures.
Es regnete, infolgedessen wir blieben zu Hause.
Es regnete. Infolgedessen blieben wir zu Hause.
"infolgedessen" starts a NEW sentence — the verb must come in Position 2, right after it, not at the end.
A comma is required before "sodass" — it introduces a subordinate clause.
After "infolgedessen", the verb must come immediately (Position 2) — not the subject first.
Sie war krank sodass ging sie nicht.
Sie war krank, sodass sie nicht ging.
Two things are missing: the comma before "sodass", and verb-final order inside the clause — "sie nicht ging", not "ging sie nicht".
Es regnete, sodass wir gingen nicht.
Es regnete, sodass wir nicht gingen.
In the "sodass"-clause, "nicht" comes before the verb, which stays at the very end: "nicht gingen".
Yeh galtiyan aksar isliye hoti hain ki dono structures ka word order mila diya jaata hai — "sodass" ke baad verb end mein jaata hai, par "infolgedessen" ke baad verb turant aata hai.
Both structures appear frequently in Goethe B2 reports, presentations, and workplace writing.
Memory trick: sodass = one sentence, verb at the END. infolgedessen = new sentence, verb in Position 2. Need a subordinate clause? Use sodass. Need a formal independent sentence? Use infolgedessen.
Dono Goethe B2 ke reports, presentations aur workplace writing mein aksar aate hain, isliye dono ka word order pakka karna zaroori hai.

The verb must go to the END of the indem-clause: "Deutsch lerne", not "lerne Deutsch".

The subject "ich" cannot be dropped inside the indem-clause.

There is no main clause here — both "indem" and "weil" open subordinate clauses, so the sentence never finishes. One clause must be a main clause. (indem and weil CAN appear in the same sentence, as long as a main clause carries them.)

Watch the punctuation carefully: dadurch belongs to the main clause, so there is NO comma before it. The comma comes only before dass, and the dass-clause has verb-final word order — Wir sparen Zeit dadurch, dass wir online arbeiten. (If the clause is fronted instead, it becomes Dadurch, dass wir online arbeiten, sparen wir Zeit.)

Punctuation dhyaan se dekho. dadurch main clause ka hissa hai, isliye uske pehle comma nahi lagta — comma sirf dass se pehle aata hai, aur dass-clause ka verb sentence ke end mein jaata hai: Wir sparen Zeit dadurch, dass wir online arbeiten. Agar clause ko aage rakho to Dadurch, dass wir online arbeiten, sparen wir Zeit.
Both answer "Wie?" — but they differ in directness and formality.
More direct — describes the method itself
Focuses on the mechanism or means

Ich verbessere mein Deutsch dadurch, dass ich regelmäßig Podcasts höre.
Dono hi "kaise?" ka jawaab dete hain. Fark itna hai ki indem seedha tareeka batata hai aur bolchaal mein natural lagta hai, jabki dadurch, dass mechanism par zor deta hai aur zyada formal lagta hai.
Never confuse means with reason — they answer different questions.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Deutschland arbeiten möchte.
Ich verbessere mein Deutsch dadurch, dass ich täglich spreche.
Means aur reason ko mila mat do. weil batata hai kyun, aur dadurch, dass batata hai kis cheez ke zariye — dono alag sawaal hain.

The verb must go to the END of the "dass"-clause: "Deutsch lernen", not "lernen Deutsch". This fragment also needs a main clause to complete the sentence.
Ich verbessere mein Deutsch dadurch ich lese.
Ich verbessere mein Deutsch dadurch, dass ich lese.
"dadurch" must be followed by ", dass" — you cannot drop "dass" and attach the clause directly.
Dadurch, dass sie viel lernt verbessert sie ihr Deutsch.
Dadurch, dass sie viel lernt, verbessert sie ihr Deutsch.
A comma is required after the "dadurch, dass"-clause, before the main clause.
Ich lerne Deutsch, dadurch dass ich nach Deutschland möchte.
Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich nach Deutschland möchte.
A wish/goal is a REASON, not a means — use "weil", not "dadurch, dass".
Dadurch, dass ich will Arzt werden.
Ich werde Arzt dadurch, dass ich das Studium abschließe.
"dadurch, dass" needs a real mechanism (an action), not a wish — and the sentence needs a main clause.

"ohne ... zu" means "without doing something." It answers: what happened WITHOUT another action?
Anna ging nach Hause, ohne sich zu verabschieden.
Rohan bestand die Prüfung, ohne viel zu lernen.
"ohne ... zu" ka matlab hai "kuch kiye bina". Yeh batata hai ki kaam ho gaya, par ek doosra action kiye bina.
Main clause, comma, "ohne" + the omitted action as an infinitive with "zu" at the end.
Pehle main clause aata hai, phir comma, phir "ohne", aur jo kaam nahi hua woh infinitive ban kar "zu" ke saath sentence ke end mein aata hai.

The ohne … zu infinitive has no subject of its own, so it borrows the subject of the main clause — both actions belong to the same person. Careful: an object inside the clause is perfectly fine. Anna geht, ohne Rohan etwas zu sagen is correct German, because Rohan is the person being told, not the one doing the leaving. Only a second subject forces you to switch to ohne dass.
Anna geht, ohne etwas zu sagen. (Anna does both actions)
Anna geht, ohne Rohan etwas sagt. (a second subject cannot take a finite verb here)

ohne … zu wale infinitive ka apna subject nahi hota, isliye woh main clause ka subject use karta hai — matlab dono kaam ek hi banda karta hai. Ek baat dhyaan mein rakho: clause ke andar object aa sakta hai. Anna geht, ohne Rohan etwas zu sagen bilkul sahi hai, kyunki Rohan ko bataya jaa raha hai — jaa Anna hi rahi hai. Sirf doosra subject aaye to ohne dass par jaana padta hai.
When subjects differ, use "ohne dass" + a full subordinate clause instead — this chapter only compares it briefly.
Anna geht, ohne etwas zu sagen.
Anna geht, ohne dass Rohan etwas sagt.
Jab dono clauses ke subject alag ho jaayein, to "ohne dass" ke saath poora subordinate clause lagta hai. Yahan ise sirf compare ke liye dikhaya gaya hai.

Both forms are correct. "statt ... zu" is more common in everyday German; "anstatt ... zu" is slightly more formal.
Main clause, comma, "(an)statt" + the alternative action as an infinitive with "zu" at the end.
Pehle main clause aata hai, phir comma, phir "(an)statt", aur jo kaam uski jagah chhoda gaya woh infinitive ban kar "zu" ke saath sentence ke end mein aata hai.

The (an)statt … zu infinitive has no subject of its own, so it takes the subject of the main clause — the same person does both. If the second action genuinely has a different subject, you need a full clause with anstatt dass: Anna lernt Deutsch, anstatt dass Rohan fernsieht. (An object inside the clause is fine, as with ohne … zu.)
Anna lernt Deutsch, anstatt fernzusehen. (Anna does both actions)
Anna lernt Deutsch, anstatt Rohan fernsieht. (a second subject needs anstatt dass)

(an)statt … zu wale infinitive ka apna subject nahi hota, isliye woh main clause ka subject le leta hai — matlab dono kaam ek hi banda karta hai. Agar doosre action ka subject sach mein alag hai, to poora clause banana padta hai anstatt dass ke saath: Anna lernt Deutsch, anstatt dass Rohan fernsieht.
Never confuse "instead of" with "without" — they express different relationships.
Ich ging, ohne etwas zu sagen. — I left without saying anything.
Ich ging, anstatt etwas zu sagen. — Instead of saying something, I left.
In dono ko mila mat do. ohne ... zu matlab kaam bina hua, aur (an)statt ... zu matlab uski jagah kuch aur hua — yani ek replacement hai.

"nicht nur ... sondern auch" means "not only ... but also ...". It introduces additional information while emphasizing the second element.
Anna spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Französisch.
Rohan arbeitet nicht nur tagsüber, sondern auch am Wochenende.
"nicht nur ... sondern auch" ka matlab hai "sirf yeh hi nahi, balki woh bhi". Yeh ek extra baat jodta hai, aur zor doosri cheez par padta hai.
Pattern yeh hai: nicht nur ke baad pehli cheez, phir comma, phir sondern auch, aur uske baad doosri cheez.
Ich mag nicht nur Kaffee, sondern auch Tee.
Anna liest nicht nur Romane, sondern auch Zeitungen.

"nicht nur ... sondern auch" can connect nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, or prepositional phrases.
nicht nur Bücher, sondern auch Zeitschriften
nicht nur lesen, sondern auch schreiben
nicht nur freundlich, sondern auch hilfsbereit

Isse tum nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs ya poore prepositional phrases jod sakte ho. Bas dono taraf ek hi tarah ka element rakhna hai.
"nicht nur ... sondern auch" vs "sowohl ... als auch"
Both connect two true elements, but the emphasis differs.
Anna spricht sowohl Deutsch als auch Englisch.
Anna spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Englisch.
Dono hi do sachchi baaton ko jodte hain, par zor alag jagah padta hai. sowohl ... als auch mein dono barabar hote hain, aur nicht nur ... sondern auch mein doosri cheez zyada important lagti hai.
German word order remains normal (V2), even when "nicht nur" starts the sentence.
Nicht nur Anna, sondern auch Rohan kommt heute.
Die Firma produziert nicht nur Autos, sondern auch Motorräder.

Word order par koi asar nahi padta — verb apni normal doosri position par hi rehta hai, chahe sentence nicht nur se shuru ho. Aur verb doosre element se agree karta hai: Nicht nur Anna, sondern auch Rohan kommt.

"nicht nur ... sondern auch" is very common in newspaper articles, reports, academic writing, presentations, and workplace communication. It creates more dynamic and persuasive writing.
These mistakes come from combining "nicht nur" with "und auch"/"aber auch", or dropping half the phrase.
Nicht nur Anna, und auch Rohan kommt.
Nicht nur Anna, sondern auch Rohan kommt.
"nicht nur" is always completed by "sondern auch" — "und auch" cannot replace it. (Note the verb agrees with the SECOND element, so it stays singular here: Rohan kommt.)
Ich mag nicht nur Kaffee, auch Tee.
Ich mag nicht nur Kaffee, sondern auch Tee.
"sondern" cannot be dropped — the fixed phrase is "sondern auch", not "auch" on its own.
Anna spricht nicht nur Deutsch aber auch Englisch.
Anna spricht nicht nur Deutsch, sondern auch Englisch.
"aber" cannot replace "sondern" in this fixed phrase.
Nicht nur ich mag Kaffee sondern Tee.
Ich mag nicht nur Kaffee, sondern auch Tee.
"nicht nur" should directly precede the first connected element, and "auch" cannot be dropped after "sondern".
Nicht nur Anna sondern Rohan auch kommt.
Nicht nur Anna, sondern auch Rohan kommt.
"auch" belongs directly after "sondern", not at the end of the clause.
Yeh galtiyan do wajah se hoti hain — sondern auch ki jagah und auch ya aber auch laga dena, ya phir sondern ya auch mein se ek chhod dena. Poora phrase saath aata hai.

In spoken German, Perfekt dominates. But sein, haben, and modal verbs often stay in Präteritum.

Written texts often begin in Präteritum. Direct speech returns to spoken German — even inside a Präteritum narration.
Anna kam nach Hause. Sie sagte: "Ich habe heute viel gelernt."

Each of these switches tense in a way the timeline does not support, or keeps a verb in a tense that sounds wrong for its register. Note that changing tense between sentences is not itself an error — it only becomes one when the context has not changed.
Anna kam nach Hause. Sie sagte: "Ich lernte heute viel."
Anna kam nach Hause. Sie sagte: "Ich habe heute viel gelernt."
Inside direct speech the register switches back to spoken German, so Perfekt is used — even when the narration around it is in Präteritum.
Gestern bin ich nach Berlin gefahren. Dort ist das Wetter wunderbar gewesen.
Gestern bin ich nach Berlin gefahren. Dort war das Wetter wunderbar.
In spoken narration the surrounding verbs take Perfekt, but sein stays in Präteritum — war, not ist gewesen.
Ich habe viel gearbeitet. Ich habe früh schlafen gemusst.
Ich habe viel gearbeitet. Ich musste früh schlafen.
Modal verbs stay in Präteritum in spoken narration — and with a dependent infinitive the Perfekt would need the Ersatzinfinitiv anyway, never gemusst.
Heute arbeite ich im Büro. Gestern arbeite ich zu Hause.
Heute arbeite ich im Büro. Gestern habe ich zu Hause gearbeitet.
The time word decides the tense: gestern needs a past form, so the tense has to follow the timeline.
Letztes Jahr bin ich Anfänger gewesen. Jetzt lernte ich Deutsch.
Letztes Jahr war ich Anfänger. Jetzt lerne ich Deutsch.
jetzt refers to the present, so it needs Präsens — and sein again prefers war over bin gewesen.

Was ist Futur I für Vermutungen?
German often uses werden + Infinitiv NOT to express the future, but to express probably / I suppose / I assume / he must be...
Anna wird jetzt zu Hause sein.
She is probably at home now (NOT "she will be home").
German mein werden + Infinitiv ka use aksar future ke liye nahi hota, balki andaaza lagane ke liye hota hai — matlab "probably" ya "mujhe lagta hai". Yahi baat shuru mein confuse karti hai.
The speaker is guessing about a present fact that is unknown to them.
Rohan wird im Büro sein. — I think he is in the office (right now).
Yahan speaker abhi ki kisi baat ka andaaza laga raha hai, jo use pakka pata nahi hai. Isliye matlab present ka hota hai, future ka nahi.
The same grammar can mean a real future plan or a present-tense assumption — context decides.
Morgen werde ich nach Berlin fahren.
Grammar dono cases mein bilkul same rehta hai — farak sirf context se pata chalta hai. Time word dekho: morgen ho to real future, aur jetzt ya gerade ho to andaaza.
A rough scale of certainty, from knowing for sure down to a soft guess. dürfte is shown here only so you recognise where it sits — it gets its own treatment later.

These mistakes come from assuming every werden + Infinitiv sentence is about the future, or confusing it with Futur II.
Anna wird jetzt zu Hause ist.
Anna wird jetzt zu Hause sein.
After werden the second verb is always a bare infinitive (sein), never a conjugated form.
Er wird morgen arbeiten. (or) Er wird jetzt arbeiten.
Mixing "jetzt" and "morgen" in the same sentence creates a contradictory, unclear timeframe.
Er wird wohl in Berlin sein.
The infinitive cannot be dropped — werden always needs its second verb at the end of the clause, even when the meaning is just a guess.
The assumption particle (wohl, wahrscheinlich) belongs in the middle of the clause, before the infinitive — it is not tacked on at the end.
Yeh galtiyan aksar isliye hoti hain ki werden ke baad plain infinitive nahi lagaya jaata, ya woh infinitive chhod diya jaata hai, ya andaaze wala shabd galat jagah rakh diya jaata hai.

Native speakers rarely reach for werden + Infinitiv. For plans, they use Präsens plus a future-time word (morgen, nächste Woche). For guesses, they use wahrscheinlich, vermutlich, or wohl — simpler, more natural than Futur I für Vermutungen.

Warum Deutsche selten Futur I benutzen
Many learners believe German always uses werden + Infinitiv. Native speakers usually don't — they prefer Präsens or probability words.
Morgen werde ich nach Berlin fahren.

Bahut se learners sochte hain ki future ke liye hamesha werden + Infinitiv chahiye. Asal mein native speakers aksar seedha Präsens use karte hain, ya andaaze ke liye wahrscheinlich, vermutlich, wohl jaise words. Futur I galat nahi hai, bas kam aata hai.
A future time word + Präsens = future meaning.
Morgen arbeite ich von zu Hause.
Nächste Woche fliegen wir nach München.
Tarika bahut simple hai — sentence mein koi future ka time word daal do (morgen, nächste Woche) aur verb Präsens mein hi rakho. Matlab future ka ban jaata hai, aur yahi German mein sabse natural hai.
Meaning: probably. Very common, natural in everyday spoken German.

Meaning: probably, I suppose — often expresses the speaker's personal assumption. Extremely common in spoken German.
Iska matlab hai "mujhe lagta hai" — yeh speaker ka apna andaaza batata hai. Bolchaal mein yeh bahut common hai, aur yeh sentence ke beech mein baithta hai, shuru mein nahi.
Both structures are correct, but the natural alternatives sound more like everyday native speech.
Er ist wohl krank. (more natural in conversation)
Dono hi sahi German hain — farak sirf yeh hai ki alternatives rozmarra ki baat mein zyada natural lagte hain, aur Futur I thoda formal ya emphatic lagta hai.

These are genuine errors — wrong verb position, a conjugated verb where an infinitive belongs, or two probability words stacked together. Choosing Futur I instead of Präsens is NOT an error: Morgen werde ich arbeiten is correct, just more formal than Morgen arbeite ich.
When a time word opens the sentence it takes position 1, so the verb must follow immediately in position 2 — before the subject.

After werden the last verb must be a bare infinitive (gehen), never a conjugated form. (Both this and the simpler Präsens version — Morgen gehe ich einkaufen — are correct German; the Präsens one is just more common.)
Wahrscheinlich kommt er. (or) Er kommt wohl.
Combining two probability markers ("wahrscheinlich" and "wohl") in one sentence is redundant — use only one.
The verb must stay in second position — "vermutlich" occupies position 1, so the verb follows immediately.
"wohl" is a modal particle that sits mid-sentence, not at the very start pushing the subject out of position 1.

Yeh sach mein galtiyan hain — verb galat position par, infinitive ki jagah conjugated form, ya do probability words ek saath. Ek baat clear rakho: Futur I use karna galti nahi hai. Morgen werde ich arbeiten sahi hai, bas Morgen arbeite ich zyada common hai.
Choosing the natural alternative over Futur I is a hallmark of fluent, native-like Goethe B2 speaking and writing.
Memory trick: Native Germans usually say "Morgen fahre ich," not "Morgen werde ich fahren." For guesses, reach for wahrscheinlich, vermutlich, or wohl before Futur I.
Futur I ki jagah natural alternative chunna B2 par kaafi natural lagta hai — speaking aur writing dono mein isse farak padta hai.

Was ist Konjunktiv II der Vergangenheit?
It describes an unreal past: reality happened one way, but the speaker wishes it had happened differently.

As soon as a modal verb joins in, the pattern changes: there is NO Partizip II at all. You get hätte + the main verb as an infinitive + the modal as an infinitive, and the modal comes LAST. This is the Ersatzinfinitiv you met in the Perfekt — the modal never appears as gesollt or gekonnt.

Note that hätte is used even with sein-verbs here: Ihr hättet … sein müssen, not wärt. The modal decides the auxiliary, so it is always hätte. In a subordinate clause the whole cluster stays together and the finite verb moves to the FRONT of it: …, dass ich besser hätte lernen sollen.

Jaise hi modal verb aata hai, pattern badal jaata hai — Partizip II bilkul nahi lagta. Structure banta hai hätte + asli verb ka infinitive + modal ka infinitive, aur modal sabse end mein aata hai. Yeh wahi Ersatzinfinitiv hai jo tumne Perfekt mein dekha tha, isliye gesollt ya gekonnt kabhi nahi aata. Ek baat dhyaan se — yahan sein wale verbs ke saath bhi hätte hi lagta hai: Ihr hättet vorsichtiger sein müssen, wärt nahi. Auxiliary modal decide karta hai. Aur subordinate clause mein poora cluster saath rehta hai, bas finite verb uske aage chala jaata hai: …, dass ich besser hätte lernen sollen.

Was ist Konjunktiv II für Vermutungen?
German often uses dürfte (probably, likely) and könnte (might, could possibly) to express assumptions when the speaker doesn't know for certain.
Anna dürfte jetzt zu Hause sein. — Anna is probably at home.
Rohan könnte krank sein. — Rohan might be ill.

Structure: Main clause + als ob + Konjunktiv II, with the verb at the very end.
Er spricht, als ob er alles wüsste.
Anna lacht, als ob sie keine Sorgen hätte.
Der Mann läuft, als ob er es eilig hätte.
Structure yeh hai: pehle main clause, phir comma, phir als ob, aur uske clause ka verb Konjunktiv II mein sentence ke end mein jaata hai.
Almost the same meaning as als ob, but mostly spoken and slightly less common.
Sie tut so, als wenn sie alles wüsste.
Rohan spricht, als wenn er Professor wäre.
Iska matlab als ob jaisa hi hai, bas yeh zyada-tar bolne mein aata hai aur kam common hai. Likhne mein als ob hi behtar rehta hai.
Many native speakers shorten the structure: the verb moves directly after "als" instead of waiting for "ob".
Er sieht aus, als wäre er müde.
Sie spricht, als hätte sie keine Zeit.
Es klingt, als käme der Zug gleich.
Native speakers is structure ko chhota kar dete hain — ob hata dete hain aur verb seedha als ke turant baad aa jaata hai. Isliye als wäre er müde mein verb end mein nahi, shuru mein hai.
All three structures express the same meaning but differ slightly in formality.

Er spricht als ob er weiß alles.

The verb after "als ob" must be in Konjunktiv II ("wüsste"), not Präsens indicative ("weiß"), and must go to the end.
Anna sieht aus als sie krank ist.
Anna sieht aus, als ob sie krank wäre. (or) Anna sieht aus, als wäre sie krank.
A comparison of appearance needs "als ob" or the shortened "als + Konjunktiv II" — not a plain "als" + indicative clause.
Er spricht als ob er ist Lehrer.
Er spricht, als ob er Lehrer wäre.
The verb must be Konjunktiv II ("wäre"), not Präsens indicative ("ist"), and must move to the end after "als ob".
Er tut so, als ob er krank war.
Er tut so, als ob er krank wäre.
Use Konjunktiv II (wäre), not Präteritum indicative (war) — this is an unreal comparison, not a statement about the real past.
Er spricht, wie ob er ein Lehrer wäre.
Er spricht, als ob er ein Lehrer wäre.
The unreal comparison uses "als ob", never "wie ob". Keep "wie" for a straightforward comparison — Er spricht wie ein Lehrer is correct German too, but it says he really does sound like one.
Yeh galtiyan do wajah se hoti hain — als ob ke baad Konjunktiv II ki jagah normal Präsens ya Präteritum laga dena, ya verb ko clause ke end mein na bhejna.

Structure: Main Clause + während + Nebensatz, verb at the end.
Anna lernt Deutsch, während Rohan arbeitet.
Während Anna kocht, liest Rohan ein Buch.

Structure simple hai: pehle main clause, phir comma, phir während, aur uske clause ka verb sentence ke end mein jaata hai. Clause ko aage bhi rakh sakte ho — phir main clause apne verb se shuru hoga.

At B2 you will meet a second meaning of während: it also marks a CONTRAST between two things, the way English uses “whereas”. The grammar is identical — verb at the end of the clause — so only the context tells you which reading is meant.
Ich höre Musik, während ich lerne. — both happening together
Anna lernt gern Grammatik, während Rohan lieber spricht. — comparing two people
Anna lernt Deutsch, während Rohan arbeitet.
In written and academic German the contrast reading is very common — it is a more elegant alternative to aber when you compare two facts.

B2 par während ka ek doosra matlab bhi milta hai — yeh contrast bhi batata hai, jaise English mein "whereas". Grammar bilkul same rehta hai, verb clause ke end mein hi jaata hai, isliye farak sirf context se pata chalta hai. Jaise Anna lernt gern Grammatik, während Rohan lieber spricht — yahan time ki baat nahi ho rahi, do logon ki comparison ho rahi hai. Written aur academic German mein yeh use bahut common hai, kyunki aber se zyada elegant lagta hai.
während shows two parallel timelines; seitdem shows a single timeline continuing to now.
Timeline ki tarah socho — während mein do lines saath-saath chalti hain, aur seitdem mein ek hi line past se shuru hokar aaj tak aati hai.

Both connectors put two actions in order — the difference is which one the CLAUSE describes. With bevor, the clause names the LATER action (so the main clause happens first). With nachdem, the clause names the EARLIER, already-completed action (so the main clause happens second).
Main clause happens FIRST; the bevor-clause action comes after
The nachdem-clause action happens FIRST and is finished; the main clause follows

Dono connectors do kaamon ko order mein rakhte hain — farak sirf itna hai ki clause kaunse kaam ki baat kar raha hai. bevor ke saath clause baad wale kaam ki baat karta hai, isliye main clause pehle hota hai. Aur nachdem ke saath clause pehle wale kaam ki baat karta hai, jo already poora ho chuka hai.
Structure: Main Clause + bevor + Nebensatz, verb at the end.
Ich frühstücke, bevor ich zur Arbeit gehe.
Bevor Anna die Präsentation hält, übt sie zu Hause.
Rohan liest den Bericht, bevor er eine Entscheidung trifft.
Structure yeh hai: pehle main clause, phir comma, phir bevor, aur uske clause ka verb sentence ke end mein. Clause ko aage bhi rakh sakte ho — phir main clause apne verb se shuru hoga.
One action is completed, then another happens. Usually pairs Plusquamperfekt (earlier action) with Präteritum/Perfekt (later action).
Nachdem Anna die Prüfung bestanden hatte, feierte sie mit ihren Freunden.
Nachdem wir gegessen hatten, gingen wir spazieren.
Nachdem Rohan die E-Mail gelesen hatte, antwortete er sofort.
Yahan ek kaam poora ho jaata hai, phir doosra hota hai. Isliye pehle wale kaam ke liye aksar Plusquamperfekt aata hai, aur baad wale ke liye Präteritum ya Perfekt.
The earlier action is often Plusquamperfekt; the later action is Präteritum or Perfekt depending on context. Spoken German often uses Perfekt.
Nachdem Anna die Hausaufgaben gemacht hatte, ging sie schlafen.
Nachdem wir angekommen waren, haben wir gegessen.
Pehla kaam aksar Plusquamperfekt mein hota hai, aur doosra context ke hisaab se Präteritum ya Perfekt mein. Bolchaal mein log zyada-tar Perfekt hi use karte hain.
bevor points to a future/planned order; nachdem points to a past order.
bevor aksar aage ki planning wale sentences mein aata hai, aur nachdem zyada-tar past ki kahani sunate waqt — kyunki wahan ek kaam pehle se poora ho chuka hota hai.

Bevor ich gegessen hatte, ging ich schlafen.
Bevor ich schlafen ging, hatte ich gegessen. (or) Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich schlafen.
"bevor" does not pair with Plusquamperfekt in this way — this sentence actually describes "after", so "nachdem" is correct.

Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, ging ich spazieren.
When the nachdem-clause comes first it fills position 1, so the main clause must start with its verb — before the subject.
Bevor ich zur Arbeit gehen, frühstücke ich.
Bevor ich zur Arbeit gehe, frühstücke ich.
Inside the bevor-clause the verb still agrees with its subject (ich → gehe) and sits at the end — it is not an infinitive.
Bevor ich gehe, räume ich auf.
"bevor" only opens a subordinate clause, so on its own the sentence is unfinished — it still needs a main clause.

dessen/deren replace a possessive article (sein/ihr) inside a relative clause.
Anna hat einen Bruder. Sein Auto ist neu.
Anna hat einen Bruder, dessen Auto neu ist.
dessen aur deren relative clause ke andar possessive ki jagah lete hain — matlab jahan tum normally sein ya ihr kehte, wahan yeh aate hain. Inka matlab hai "jiska" ya "jiski".
Used when the possessed noun belongs to a masculine or neuter antecedent.
Der Mann, dessen Auto gestohlen wurde, ist mein Nachbar.
Das Kind, dessen Eltern Ärzte sind, wohnt nebenan.
Der Professor, dessen Vortrag interessant war, arbeitet an der Universität.
dessen tab aata hai jab comma se pehle wala noun masculine ya neuter ho — matlab der ya das wala.
Used when the possessed noun belongs to a feminine or plural antecedent.
Die Frau, deren Sohn Arzt ist, arbeitet hier.
Die Studenten, deren Prüfung morgen beginnt, lernen gemeinsam.
Die Firma, deren Produkte weltweit verkauft werden, expandiert weiter.
deren tab aata hai jab comma se pehle wala noun feminine ho ya plural — matlab dono cases mein die wala.
Memorize this table — the antecedent's gender/number decides the choice.
Is table ko yaad kar lo. Yaad rakhne ki ek hi baat hai — choice comma se pehle wale noun se hoti hai, uske baad wale noun se nahi. Yahi sabse badi galti hoti hai.

Once you have picked dessen or deren from the antecedent, the form never changes again — no matter what job the possessed noun does inside the relative clause. It can be the subject, the accusative object, or sit after a preposition; dessen stays dessen.
Two more things follow from this: the possessed noun takes no article of its own (dessen Auto, never dessen das Auto), and any adjective in front of it takes a strong ending (dessen neues Auto).
Der Mann, dessen Auto neu ist, …
Der Mann, dessen Auto ich gesehen habe, …
Der Mann, mit dessen Bruder ich arbeite, …
Die Frau, deren Sohn ich kenne, …
Note the third row: when a preposition is involved it comes FIRST, before dessen/deren — mit dessen Bruder, not dessen mit Bruder.

Ek baar antecedent dekh kar dessen ya deren choose kar liya, to woh form phir badalta nahi — chahe uske baad wala noun subject ho, object ho, ya preposition ke baad aaye. Isliye dessen Auto neu ist aur dessen Auto ich gesehen habe — dono mein dessen hi rehta hai. Do baatein saath yaad rakho: us noun par apna koi article nahi lagta (dessen Auto, na ki dessen das Auto), aur agar adjective aaye to usme strong ending lagti hai (dessen neues Auto). Aur preposition ho to woh sabse pehle aata hai: mit dessen Bruder.
sein/ihr cannot be used inside a relative clause — dessen/deren must replace them.
Der Mann, sein Auto gestohlen wurde...
Der Mann, dessen Auto gestohlen wurde...
Relative clause ke andar sein ya ihr nahi chalta — wahan dessen ya deren hi aata hai. Yeh dono hi possessive ka kaam kar dete hain, isliye alag se sein lagane ki zaroorat nahi.
dessen and deren are extremely common in newspapers, reports, academic writing, presentations, and business communication.
They make writing more elegant and compact — a strong marker of formal, native-like B2 German.
dessen aur deren newspapers, reports aur business writing mein bahut aate hain, kyunki inse do sentences ek saaf sentence ban jaate hain. Isliye reading mein inhe pehchaanna zaroori hai.
These mistakes come from using sein/ihr instead of dessen/deren, or choosing the wrong one based on the possessed noun instead of the antecedent.
Der Mann, sein Auto neu ist...
Der Mann, dessen Auto neu ist...
"sein" cannot be used inside a relative clause — "dessen" replaces it.
Die Frau, dessen Sohn Arzt ist...
Die Frau, deren Sohn Arzt ist...
The antecedent "die Frau" is feminine, so "deren" is required — not "dessen".
Das Kind, deren Eltern hier wohnen...
Das Kind, dessen Eltern hier wohnen...
The antecedent "das Kind" is neuter, so "dessen" is required — not "deren".
Die Studenten, dessen Prüfung morgen ist...
Die Studenten, deren Prüfung morgen ist...
The antecedent "die Studenten" is plural, so "deren" is required — not "dessen".
Der Professor, der sein Vortrag interessant war...
Der Professor, dessen Vortrag interessant war...
A possessive relationship requires "dessen", not a plain relative pronoun "der" plus "sein".
Yeh galtiyan do wajah se hoti hain — sein/ihr ko relative clause mein use kar dena, ya dessen/deren ka choice galat noun dekh kar karna. Choice hamesha comma se pehle wale noun se hoti hai.
Always ask: what is the antecedent (the noun right before the comma)? Its gender/number decides dessen vs deren.
Memory trick: der/das → dessen. die/die(Pl.) → deren. Think: Whose? → Use dessen/deren.
Har baar ek hi sawaal poochho — comma se pehle wala noun kya hai? Uska gender aur number hi tay karta hai ki dessen aayega ya deren.

German mein aksar ek relative clause doosre ke andar aa jaata hai, ya ek hi sentence mein kai relative clauses jud jaate hain. Reading mein yeh dikhte hain, isliye inhe tod kar padhna aana chahiye.
Schritt für Schritt aufbauen (Building Step by Step)
Start with the main sentence, then add relative clauses one at a time.
Der Professor arbeitet an der Universität.
Der Professor, der an der Universität arbeitet, ...
Der Professor, der an der Universität arbeitet, deren Bibliothek modern ist, ...
Aise sentences banane ka tarika yeh hai — pehle simple main sentence likho, phir ek-ek karke relative clause jodo. Ek saath sab likhne ki koshish mein hi galti hoti hai.
Rule: every relative pronoun belongs to exactly ONE noun. Always ask: which noun does this pronoun describe?
Die Studentin, deren Bruder, der in München lebt, Ingenieur ist...

Ek rule yaad rakho — har relative pronoun sirf ek noun se juda hota hai. Isliye jab bhi confuse ho, ruk kar poochho: yeh pronoun kis noun ki baat kar raha hai? Wahi noun uska gender aur number tay karta hai.
The hierarchy: main clause → relative clause → nested relative clause → main clause continues.
Main Clause → Relative Clause → Nested Relative Clause → Main Clause continues
Structure ko layers ki tarah socho — main clause shuru hota hai, uske andar relative clause aata hai, uske andar ek aur, aur phir main clause wahin se aage badhta hai jahan ruka tha.
Never read nested relative clauses word by word. Follow this strategy instead.

One nested clause is natural. Three or four is usually too difficult for the reader.
Elegant B2 writing uses nesting sparingly — clarity matters more than complexity.
Padhne ke liye inhe samajhna zaroori hai, par khud likhte waqt ek nested clause hi kaafi hai. Teen-chaar levels reader ke liye bhaari ho jaate hain — tab do simple sentences behtar rehte hain.

These come from breaking verb-final order inside a nested clause, attaching a pronoun to the wrong noun, dropping the commas that mark the inner clause, leaving the main clause unfinished, or taking the case from the wrong verb.
Der Mann, dessen Tochter, die studiert in Berlin, Ärztin ist, arbeitet hier.
Der Mann, dessen Tochter, die in Berlin studiert, Ärztin ist, arbeitet hier.
A nested relative clause is still a subordinate clause, so its verb goes to the very end — die in Berlin studiert, not die studiert in Berlin.
Der Professor, der an der Universität arbeitet, dessen Bibliothek modern ist, ist bekannt.
Der Professor, der an der Universität arbeitet, deren Bibliothek modern ist, ist bekannt.
The second pronoun points back to die Universität, which is feminine — so it must be deren, not dessen. In a nested sentence always check which noun each pronoun actually attaches to.
Die Studentin, deren Bruder der in München lebt Ingenieur ist, kommt heute.
Die Studentin, deren Bruder, der in München lebt, Ingenieur ist, kommt heute.
Every nested clause needs a comma on BOTH sides. Without them the reader cannot see where the inner clause starts and stops.
Der Mann, der dort steht, Lehrer.
Der Mann, der dort steht, ist Lehrer.
Once the relative clause closes, the main clause still has to finish — it needs its own verb (ist).
Der Kollege, den ich vertraue, arbeitet in dem Büro, das neu ist.
Der Kollege, dem ich vertraue, arbeitet in dem Büro, das neu ist.
vertrauen takes the Dativ, so the pronoun is dem. Each clause picks its case from its OWN verb, not from the main clause.

Was sind Relativsätze mit wer... der...?
"wer" opens a clause about anyone at all — there is no specific antecedent noun.
Wer wagt, gewinnt. — Whoever dares, wins.
"wer" ka matlab hai "jo koi bhi". Yahan koi khaas noun nahi hota jiski baat ho — baat kisi bhi aise insaan ki hoti hai jo woh kaam kare. Isliye yeh proverbs mein bahut aata hai.
The "wer" clause sends the verb to the end, like any Nebensatz. Then der/die/das resumes the main clause.
Wer zu spät kommt, den bestraft das Leben.
Wer ein Gemälde stiehlt, der braucht einen Käufer.
"wer" wala clause bhi Nebensatz hai, isliye uska verb end mein jaata hai. Uske baad comma, aur phir der/die/das se main clause shuru hota hai — yeh pronoun baat ko aage uthata hai.
Der Fall kann sich ändern (The Case Can Change)
The resuming pronoun (der/die/das/den/dem/dessen/deren) takes whatever case the MAIN clause verb requires — this can differ from "wer"'s own case.

Yahan sabse important baat hai. Resuming pronoun apna case main clause ke verb se leta hai, "wer" se nahi. Isliye "wer" Nominativ mein hote hue bhi aage den ya dem aa sakta hai — yeh main clause ka verb tay karta hai.
Wenn der Nominativ passt (When Nominativ Fits)
If the main clause also needs Nominativ, the resuming pronoun can sometimes be omitted or matches directly.
Wer wagt, gewinnt. (no separate pronoun needed)
Wer ein Gemälde stiehlt, der braucht einen Käufer. (der = Nom., matches)
Agar main clause ko bhi Nominativ hi chahiye, to pronoun aur "wer" ka case ek jaisa ho jaata hai. Aise case mein pronoun chhoda bhi jaa sakta hai — Wer wagt, gewinnt — ya rakha bhi jaa sakta hai.
This structure is extremely common in proverbs, general truths, and formal/written German.
Think of famous German proverbs — most use exactly this wer...der... pattern.
Yeh structure proverbs aur general baaton mein bahut aata hai, aur formal writing mein bhi. German ke mashhoor proverbs zyada-tar isi pattern par bane hain.
These come from giving the resuming pronoun the wrong case, dropping the comma, or putting the pronoun in the wrong slot in the main clause.
Wer zu spät kommt, der bestraft das Leben.
Wer zu spät kommt, den bestraft das Leben.
Here das Leben is the subject and it does the punishing — the person arriving late is the OBJECT. Since bestrafen takes the Akkusativ, the resuming pronoun is den, not der.
A comma always separates the wer-clause from the main clause — even in a short proverb like this one.
Wer ein Gemälde stiehlt, braucht der einen Käufer.
Wer ein Gemälde stiehlt, der braucht einen Käufer.
The resuming pronoun opens the main clause, so it comes straight after the comma — before the verb, not after it.
Wer zittert hat etwas zu verbergen.
Wer zittert, hat etwas zu verbergen.

The only thing missing is the comma. The verb is already at the end of the wer-clause, and because the main clause also needs a Nominativ subject, no resuming der is required — though …, der hat etwas zu verbergen is equally correct.
Yeh galtiyan teen wajah se hoti hain — resuming pronoun ko galat case dena, comma chhod dena, ya us pronoun ko main clause mein galat jagah rakhna.

German has TWO important passive structures. Vorgangspassiv describes the action happening; Zustandspassiv describes the finished result — the state that remains.

German mein passive ke do roop hain. Vorgangspassiv (werden ke saath) batata hai ki kaam ho raha hai, aur Zustandspassiv (sein ke saath) batata hai ki kaam ho chuka hai aur ab kya haalat hai. Ek process hai, doosra result.
Zustandspassiv is built with a conjugated form of "sein" plus the Partizip II — the same participle used in Vorgangspassiv and Perfekt, but now paired with sein.
Yeh sein ke conjugated form aur Partizip II se banta hai. Participle wahi rehta hai jo Perfekt mein aata hai — sirf helper badalta hai. Isliye naya kuch yaad nahi karna, bas sein lagana hai.
Compare the same participle with werden (process) and sein (result) side by side.
Ek hi participle ko dono helpers ke saath dekho — werden ke saath kaam chal raha hai, aur sein ke saath kaam khatam ho gaya hai. Yahi poora farak hai.
Zustandspassiv appears constantly in realistic workplace and travel situations.
Yeh structure office aur travel wale situations mein bahut aata hai — jaise notice board par ya email mein, jahan sirf current haalat batani hoti hai.
Zustandspassiv focuses ONLY on the current condition. It does NOT say who performed the action or when — that information is simply absent from the sentence.

Zustandspassiv sirf abhi ki haalat batata hai. Isme yeh nahi hota ki kaam kisne kiya ya kab kiya — woh jaankaari sentence mein aati hi nahi. Agar karne wale ka naam batana ho, to Vorgangspassiv use karo.

These come from using an infinitive instead of the Partizip II, forgetting subject agreement on sein, mixing up worden and geworden, or trying to name an agent in a Zustandspassiv. Note that choosing werden instead of sein is NOT an error — Die Tür wird geöffnet and Die Tür ist geöffnet are both correct and simply mean different things.
Zustandspassiv needs the Partizip II after sein, never the infinitive.
sein still agrees with its subject — die Fenster is plural, so it takes sind.
The Perfekt of Vorgangspassiv uses worden, never geworden — geworden belongs to the verb werden meaning “to become”.
The Partizip II of "unterschreiben" is "unterschrieben", not "unterschreiben".
Das Büro ist von dem Chef geschlossen.
Das Büro ist geschlossen. / Das Büro wurde vom Chef geschlossen.
Zustandspassiv only reports the state, so it does not name who did it. If you need the agent, switch to Vorgangspassiv with wurde.

Yeh galtiyan chaar wajah se hoti hain — Partizip II ki jagah infinitive laga dena, sein ko subject se match na karna, worden aur geworden mila dena, ya Zustandspassiv mein kaam karne wale ka naam daal dena. Ek baat clear rakho: werden ki jagah sein chunna galti nahi hai — dono sahi hain, bas matlab alag hai.
Ask yourself: Am I talking about an action happening, or the result after it? That answers werden vs sein immediately.
Memory trick: werden = something is happening. sein = something is already finished. Process? → werden. Result? → sein.
Har baar khud se ek sawaal poochho — main kaam ho rahe hone ki baat kar raha hoon, ya kaam ho chukne ke baad ki haalat ki? Isi se turant pata chal jaayega ki werden lagana hai ya sein.

Sometimes there is NO object that can become the subject. German still forms a passive sentence — the speaker does NOT care WHO performs the action; only the activity matters.
People are laughing a lot today.

Kabhi-kabhi sentence mein koi aisa object hi nahi hota jo passive mein subject ban sake. German phir bhi passive bana leta hai — kyunki yahan yeh batana hi nahi hota ki kaam kaun kar raha hai, sirf kaam ki baat hoti hai.
Es wird gearbeitet — "es" occupies Position 1 by default. Once another element (heute, hier, im Büro) occupies Position 1, "es" simply disappears.
es sirf Position 1 bharne ke liye aata hai. Jaise hi koi doosri cheez (heute, hier, im Büro) Position 1 le leti hai, es gayab ho jaata hai — dono ek saath nahi rehte.
Use Unpersönliches Passiv when the person is unknown, the person is irrelevant, or you're giving rules, announcements, or describing activities.
There's no smoking in the restaurant.
Ise tab use karo jab karne wala pata na ho, ya uska pata hona zaroori na ho. Isliye yeh rules, announcements aur kisi jagah ki activity batane ke liye sabse zyada aata hai — jaise notice board par.
Es wird gefeiert (✅). Heute wird gefeiert (✅). Im Hotel wird Englisch gesprochen (✅). But: Heute wird es gefeiert (❌) — "es" cannot coexist with another Position 1 element.
Ek hi rule yaad rakho — Position 1 par ya es aayega, ya koi doosri cheez. Dono ek saath kabhi nahi aate.

Normal passive has a real subject that could receive an agent. Unpersönliches Passiv has no subject at all — only the action remains.
Es wird geschrieben. (no subject, only action)
Normal passive mein ek asli subject hota hai — koi cheez jispar kaam hua. Unpersönliches Passiv mein woh subject hi nahi hota, sirf kaam bachta hai.
Unpersönliches Passiv appears constantly in announcements, signs, newspapers, reports, academic German, business German, and public notices.

These mistakes come from misplacing "es", forgetting it must vanish, or adding an unnecessary agent.
Es wird hier gearbeitet. / Hier wird gearbeitet.
Nothing may follow the Partizip II — it closes the clause. So "hier" belongs in the middle, or it can take Position 1 instead (and then "es" drops).
"es" must disappear once "hier" occupies Position 1 — the two cannot coexist.
The passive needs Partizip II ("gesprochen"), not the bare infinitive.
The finite verb "wird" must stay in Position 2, immediately after "Heute".
Es wird gearbeitet von vielen Menschen.
Es wird gearbeitet. / Es wird von vielen Menschen gearbeitet.
Again nothing follows the Partizip II. And in practice you would simply leave the agent out — the whole point of this structure is that WHO does it does not matter.

Yeh galtiyan aksar isliye hoti hain ki es ko wahan rakh diya jaata hai jahan pehle se koi cheez Position 1 par hai, ya Partizip II ke baad kuch aur jod diya jaata hai. Yaad rakho — Partizip II sentence band kar deta hai.
Is there a subject? Use normal passive. Talking only about the action, with no WHO at all? Use Unpersönliches Passiv, and remember: "es" only ever sits in Position 1.
Memory trick: talking about WHO? → normal passive. Talking only about THE ACTION? → Unpersönliches Passiv.

You are a warm, encouraging German (B2) tutor for a Hindi/English-speaking learner. The lesson is BEKOMMEN-/KRIEGEN-/ERHALTEN-PASSIV (the recipient passive) at B2 level: Recipient + bekommen/kriegen/erhalten + Partizip II, where the RECIPIENT becomes the grammatical subject instead of the thing acted upon. Example: "Der Schüler bekommt die Grammatik erklärt" (the student gets the grammar explained), contrasted with Vorgangspassiv "Die Grammatik wird erklärt" (the grammar is explained). Register: bekommen = neutral, kriegen = informal/spoken, erhalten = formal (letters, business, academic). All three mean the same thing grammatically, but differ in register: bekommen is neutral and most common; kriegen is informal and very common in spoken German; erhalten is formal — letters, business, authorities, academic German.

Vorgangspassiv focuses on the action; bekommen-Passiv focuses on the recipient. Students must clearly distinguish these two focuses.

These mistakes come from wrong word order, mixing bekommen with werden, or using the wrong verb form.
The object comes before the Partizip II, which sits at the very end of the clause.
The subject must be the RECEIVER — someone who can actually receive something (a person, or an organisation like die Firma). The thing being sent cannot be the subject here.
Ich werde den Vertrag bekommen geschickt.
bekommen-Passiv never combines with "werden" — "bekommen" itself is the passive auxiliary here.
The verb after "bekommen" must be Partizip II ("geschickt"), never the infinitive ("schicken").
The object ("die Aufgabe") comes before the Partizip II ("erklärt"), which stays at the end.
Yeh galtiyan teen wajah se hoti hain — object aur Partizip II ka order ulta kar dena, bekommen ke saath werden jod dena, ya Partizip II ki jagah infinitive laga dena.

German often replaces modal verbs with more formal structures. haben + zu puts the RESPONSIBLE PERSON in focus: Ich habe den Bericht zu schreiben. sein + zu puts the TASK in focus, impersonally: Der Bericht ist zu schreiben.

The lesson is MODALITÄTSERSATZ: HABEN + ZU / SEIN + ZU at B2 level — formal alternatives to modal verbs (especially müssen). "haben + zu + Infinitiv" puts the RESPONSIBLE PERSON in focus (e.g. "Ich habe den Bericht zu schreiben" = I have to write the report). "sein + zu + Infinitiv" puts the TASK in focus, impersonally/passive-flavoured (e.g. "Der Bericht ist zu schreiben" = the report is to be written). With separable verbs, "zu" is inserted between the prefix and stem (e.g. "einzureichen", "mitzubringen"). Seven passive structures, one context each: Vorgangspassiv (process), Zustandspassiv (result), sich lassen (possibility), Unpersönliches Passiv (general activity), bekommen-Passiv (recipient), haben+zu (responsibility), sein+zu (task).

Professional German mixes all seven structures fluidly, choosing by what the sentence needs to emphasise — never forcing one construction everywhere.

German has two styles. Verbalstil focuses on the action; Nominalstil turns the same idea into a formal noun-based concept.

German mein likhne ke do styles hain. Verbalstil mein verb par focus hota hai — yeh normal, bolne wali German hai. Nominalstil mein wahi baat noun ke roop mein aati hai, aur tab sentence formal aur official lagta hai.
Many verbs have a natural noun equivalent, often carrying the same meaning but changing the style to formal.

Kai verbs ka apna noun form hota hai, aur matlab wahi rehta hai — bas style formal ho jaata hai. Dhyaan do ki -ung wale saare nouns feminine hote hain (die Entwicklung, die Bewerbung), isliye article yaad karna aasaan hai.
Adjective-based nouns are also extremely common in formal writing.
Adjectives se bane nouns bhi formal writing mein bahut aate hain. Yahan bhi ek pattern hai — -heit, -keit aur -tät wale sab feminine hote hain.
Comparing full sentences shows how the register shifts from everyday to formal without changing the core meaning.

Das Objekt kommt in den Genitiv
When you nominalise a verb, its object does not disappear — it moves into the Genitiv behind the new noun. This is the single most important mechanical step, and the one learners most often skip.
If the verb had a fixed preposition, that preposition stays instead of a Genitiv: sich bewerben um → die Bewerbung um die Stelle, not die Bewerbung der Stelle.

Jab tum verb ko noun banate ho, to uska object gayab nahi hota — woh naye noun ke peeche Genitiv mein chala jaata hai. Yeh sabse zaroori step hai aur yahi sabse zyada chhoot jaata hai. Masculine aur neuter mein des aata hai aur noun par ek -s bhi lagta hai (des Vertrags), aur feminine aur plural mein der (der Kommunikation, der Daten). Ek exception yaad rakho — agar verb ka apna fixed preposition tha, to woh preposition hi rehta hai: die Bewerbung um die Stelle.

The lesson is ERWEITERTE PARTIZIPIALATTRIBUTE (extended participial attributes) at B2 level: replacing relative clauses with compact attributes placed before the noun, built from Partizip I (active/ongoing, e.g. "arbeitend" → "der arbeitende Student") or Partizip II (passive/completed, e.g. "unterschrieben" → "die unterschriebenen Dokumente"). German often replaces long relative clauses with compact participial attributes, moving all the information BEFORE the noun instead of after it.
Der Student, der im Labor arbeitet,
Die Dokumente, die gestern unterschrieben wurden,

German aksar lambe relative clause ki jagah ek compact structure use karta hai. Isme saari jaankaari noun ke baad nahi, balki pehle aa jaati hai. Isliye reading mein aisa lagta hai ki article ke baad bahut kuch aa gaya aur noun kaafi der baad aaya — aur yahi ise mushkil banata hai.
Partizip I (verb stem + -end + adjective ending) expresses an ACTIVE, ongoing action — the noun is DOING something.
Partizip I banane ka tarika simple hai — infinitive ke aage seedha -d lagao (arbeiten → arbeitend), phir adjective ending. Iska matlab hota hai ki noun khud kaam kar raha hai.
Partizip II expresses a COMPLETED action or resulting state — the noun HAS BEEN acted upon.
Partizip II wahi form hai jo tum Perfekt mein use karte ho (unterschrieben, geschlossen, gekauft). Yahan iska matlab hota hai ki noun ke saath kaam ho chuka hai — isliye matlab passive lagta hai.
The "extended" version moves entire prepositional phrases, adverbs, and objects before the participle — everything that would have been in the relative clause.
Der Student, der an einem internationalen Forschungsprojekt arbeitet,
Der an einem internationalen Forschungsprojekt arbeitende Student
Die Unterlagen, die gestern vom Professor unterschrieben wurden,
Die gestern vom Professor unterschriebenen Unterlagen

"Extended" ka matlab hai ki jo bhi relative clause mein hota — prepositional phrases, adverbs, objects — woh sab participle se pehle aa jaata hai. Padhne ka tarika yeh hai: pehle article dekho, phir seedha noun dhoondo, aur beech ka hissa baad mein samjho.
Partizip I oder II? Die Entscheidung
This is the decision that matters most. Ask one question: is the noun DOING the action, or is the action being done TO it?
Doing it → Partizip I (stem + -end). Having it done to it → Partizip II. Both then take a normal adjective ending.

A small group of movement verbs works differently: with ankommen, einschlafen and similar, Partizip II describes a completed state, not a passive one — der angekommene Zug (the train that has arrived), das eingeschlafene Kind (the child that has fallen asleep).

Yahi sabse important faisla hai, aur ek hi sawaal se ho jaata hai — noun kaam kar raha hai, ya uske saath kaam ho raha hai? Agar noun khud kar raha hai to Partizip I (stem + -end): der lesende Student. Aur agar uske saath kuch kiya gaya hai to Partizip II: das gelesene Buch. Uske baad normal adjective ending lagti hai. Ek chhota exception — movement wale verbs mein Partizip II passive nahi, balki poora ho chuka state batata hai: der angekommene Zug.
Both express the same idea; the participial attribute is shorter and more formal.
Die Frau, die im Krankenhaus arbeitet,
Der Bericht, der gestern veröffentlicht wurde,
Dono ka matlab ek hi hai — participial attribute bas chhota aur zyada formal hai. Bolne mein log relative clause hi use karte hain; yeh structure zyada-tar likhne mein aata hai.

These come from choosing the wrong participle, dropping the adjective ending, using a bare infinitive, or leaving a conjugated auxiliary inside the attribute.
Partizip I (schreibend) for an ACTIVE meaning — the student is writing. Partizip II would mean the student had been written, which makes no sense.
Plural attributive adjectives need the ending "-en": "unterschriebenen", not the bare participle "unterschrieben".
The word must be the Partizip I "arbeitend" with an ending, not the bare infinitive "arbeiten".
The extended attribute never contains a conjugated auxiliary like "wurde" — only the participle with its adjective ending.
The participle needs both the correct article/gender and the attributive ending: "die entwickelte", not "das entwickelt".
Yeh galtiyan chaar wajah se hoti hain — galat participle chunna, adjective ending chhod dena, plain infinitive laga dena, ya attribute ke andar wurde jaisa conjugated verb chhod dena.
Need a short, everyday description? Use a relative clause. Need a compact, formal style? Move everything before the noun and use a Partizipialattribut.

Everyday baat mein relative clause hi use karo — woh natural lagta hai. Aur formal writing mein compact style chahiye to sab kuch noun se pehle le jaao aur Partizipialattribut use karo. Bolchaal mein ise avoid karo, warna bhaari lagta hai.

German aksar poori jaankaari ek hi noun ke aas-paas rakh deta hai, aur use layer by layer banata hai. Isliye reading mein ek sentence mein bahut kam verbs hote hain par noun phrases bahut lambe ho jaate hain.
Students must always locate the MAIN noun first — everything else modifies it.

A complex noun phrase can combine: article, quantifier, adjective(s), Partizipialattribut, Genitiv attribute, prepositional phrase.

A reliable four-step reading strategy for any long German noun phrase.

Lambe noun phrase ko padhne ka ek pakka tarika hai. Pehle head noun dhoondo, phir beech ke modifiers ko chhod do, phir unhe ek-ek karke padho, aur end mein poora matlab jodo. Shuru se seedha padhne ki koshish mein hi confusion hoti hai.
The slots are not interchangeable — German fills them in a fixed order. Everything except the Genitiv and the prepositional phrase goes BEFORE the noun; those two follow it.
Two details worth remembering: an adverb modifying a participle keeps its bare form (neu entwickelt, not neue entwickelt), and when several adjectives stack up they all take the SAME ending.

In slots ka order fix hai — tum inhe idhar-udhar nahi kar sakte. Article, Partizipialattribut aur adjectives noun se pehle aate hain, aur Genitiv aur prepositional phrase noun ke baad. Do chhoti baatein yaad rakho — participle se pehle wala adverb bina ending rehta hai (neu entwickelt, na ki neue entwickelt), aur agar kai adjectives ek saath aayein to sabki ending ek jaisi hoti hai.

These mistakes come from wrong adjective endings, wrong word order, or scattering the modifiers after the noun instead of before it.
Attributive adjectives need the full ending "-e" (with a definite article, masc. nom.), not the bare stem "wissenschaftlich".
The adverb "gestern" must sit BEFORE the participle "veröffentlichte", not after it.
When several adjectives stack up they ALL take the same ending — after "der" every one of them ends in -e, not just the last.
A Genitiv attribute comes AFTER the head noun, not before it — unlike adjectives and participles, which come before.
Before a participle, use the adverb form "neu" (not the adjective "neue") — "neu entwickelt" means "newly developed".
Yeh galtiyan chaar wajah se hoti hain — adjective ki ending galat lagana, adverb ko participle ke baad rakh dena, Genitiv ko noun se pehle le aana, ya participle se pehle adverb par ending laga dena.
Never read a long noun phrase left to right only. Find the MAIN NOUN first, then ask: who? which? what kind? from where? about what? Every other word describes that one noun.
Memory trick: complex noun phrases are a puzzle with one solution — the head noun. Find it first, then everything else falls into place.

Modal particles do NOT change the factual information in a sentence. They change emotion, expectation, politeness, surprise, or shared knowledge.
Du kommst doch. / Du kommst ja.

Modal particles sentence ki factual baat nahi badalte — baat wahi rehti hai. Yeh sirf tone badalte hain: emotion, expectation, politeness, surprise, ya yeh signal ki baat dono ko pehle se pata hai. Isliye inka koi seedha English translation nahi hota.
"doch" has five main functions: reminder, contradiction, encouragement, persuasion, and softening commands.
Du kennst ihn doch. ("you know him, remember?")
Das stimmt doch nicht! ("that's NOT true!")
Komm doch mit! ("come on, join us!")
Probier doch mal den Kuchen. ("go on, try the cake")

doch ke paanch kaam hain — yaad dilana, kisi baat ko kaatna, hosla dena, manana, aur order ko narm karna. In sab mein ek common baat hai: doch aksar us cheez ki taraf ishara karta hai jo saamne wala bhool raha hai ya maan nahi raha.
"ja" has five main functions: shared knowledge, obvious information, explanation, reminder, and surprise after realization.
Das weißt du ja. ("as you already know")
Es ist ja kalt. ("it's cold, obviously")
Er ist ja krank. ("well, he's sick, that explains it")
Du hast ja morgen Prüfung. ("remember, you have an exam tomorrow")
ja ke paanch kaam hain — pehle se pata baat batana, obvious cheez kehna, wajah samjhaana, yaad dilana, aur achanak realization. In sab ka matlab lagbhag yeh hota hai: "yeh to tum jaante hi ho".
Modal particles have a fixed home: the Mittelfeld. They come after the conjugated verb and after any pronoun, and they never take position 1 or the very end of the clause.

Never at the start and never at the end: Doch du kennst ihn and Du kennst ihn ja doch both sound wrong. Note that clause-initial doch is a different word — there it is a conjunction meaning “yet / however”.

In particles ki jagah fix hai — yeh Mittelfeld mein baithte hain, matlab conjugated verb ke baad aur pronoun ke baad. Yeh na sentence ke shuru mein aate hain aur na end mein. Perfekt ho to Partizip II se pehle aate hain: Er ist ja gekommen. Ek baat dhyaan se — sentence ke shuru wala doch alag cheez hai; wahan woh conjunction hota hai, matlab "phir bhi".
The factual meaning stays the same across all three versions — only the emotional colour changes.

Teeno versions ka factual matlab ek hi hai — sirf tone badalta hai. doch lagane se lagta hai ki tum yaad dila rahe ho ya disagree kar rahe ho, aur ja lagane se lagta hai ki baat obvious hai ya dono ko pata hai.

"doch" and "ja" are extremely common in conversations, family discussions, workplace conversations, university discussions, interviews, TV shows, and podcasts — but much less common in formal academic writing.

doch aur ja bolchaal mein bahut aate hain — baatcheet, office ki baat, interviews, TV aur podcasts mein. Par formal academic writing mein yeh lagbhag nahi aate, isliye report likhte waqt inhe chhod do.
Students should NEVER translate "doch" as "however" in every sentence, and "ja" does NOT always mean "yes". Meaning depends entirely on context.

Ek badi galti hai in particles ka seedha translation dhoondna. doch ko har jagah "however" mat samjho, aur Mittelfeld wala ja "yes" nahi hota. Inka matlab context se aata hai — isliye translate karne ki jagah yeh socho ki bolne wala kya feel karwa raha hai.
These come from stacking two particles, putting one at the start or the end instead of the Mittelfeld, or choosing the particle that carries the wrong attitude.
Ich bin Student. / Ich bin ja Student.
Do not stack the answer word and the particle. Use one "ja" in the middle field — and only when you really are pointing to shared knowledge.
"doch" appears once, in the middle field — not doubled at the start of the sentence as well.
Das stimmt doch nicht, doch es ist wahr.
Das stimmt doch nicht, aber es ist wahr.
The first "doch" is a Modalpartikel in the middle field. To join two clauses you need a conjunction — "aber" (or "doch" at the START of the clause), not a second middle-field particle.
The answer word "ja" opens the sentence, but the Modalpartikel "ja" belongs in the middle field — right after the verb, never at the end.
"doch" is the particle for a friendly invitation. "ja" in an imperative sounds like a threat — Komm ja nicht zu spät! means “don’t you dare be late”.
Yeh galtiyan teen wajah se hoti hain — do particles ek saath laga dena, particle ko Mittelfeld ki jagah shuru ya end mein rakh dena, ya galat particle chun lena jisse attitude hi badal jaata hai.
Need to remind someone? Use doch. Need to refer to shared knowledge? Use ja. Writing a scientific report? Usually use neither.

Memory trick: doch = "remember?" / "come on!" / "actually!" — often changes expectation. ja = "as you already know..." — points to shared or obvious information. Don't translate literally — understand the speaker's intention.

Faisla aasaan hai — kisi ko yaad dilana hai ya manana hai to doch. Aur yeh batana hai ki baat pehle se pata hai to ja. Scientific report likh rahe ho to dono chhod do. Aur dono ek hi Mittelfeld mein saath mat lagao.

Achhe text mein ek hi noun baar-baar nahi aata — ideas ek doosre se jude rehte hain. Isliye German mein pehli baar noun aata hai, aur uske baad uski jagah chhote shabd le lete hain.
Verweiswörter point back to something already mentioned: er, sie, es, dieser, diese, dieses, derjenige, diejenige, dasjenige, solch-, derselbe, dies, das.

Verweiswörter woh shabd hain jo pehle kahi gayi cheez ki taraf ishara karte hain — er, sie, es, dieser, diese, dieses, derjenige, solch-, derselbe, dies, das. Inme se roz kaam aane wale er/sie/es aur dieser/dies/das hi hain; baaki zyada formal writing mein aate hain.
Personal pronouns (er/sie/es) replace a previously mentioned noun, matching its gender and number.
Rohan schreibt einen Bericht. Rohan gibt den Bericht morgen ab.
Rohan schreibt einen Bericht. Er gibt ihn morgen ab.
Personal pronouns (er/sie/es) us noun ki jagah lete hain jo pehle aa chuka hai, aur uske gender aur number se match karte hain. Yeh sabse aam tarika hai repetition se bachne ka.
A Verweiswort has to match its antecedent in gender and number, but it takes its case from its own new sentence. These are two separate decisions, and the case is the one learners forget.
So der Bericht becomes er or ihn depending on the job it does next — the gender stays masculine either way.

Verweiswort ko do cheezein dekhni padti hain. Gender aur number us noun se aate hain jiski baat ho rahi hai, par case naye sentence se aata hai — matlab us pronoun ka apna kaam kya hai. Yahi doosri baat aksar chhoot jaati hai. Isliye der Bericht subject bane to er, aur object bane to ihn — gender dono mein masculine hi rehta hai.
Demonstrative pronouns (dieser/diese/dieses) create a clearer, more emphatic reference than a plain personal pronoun.
Die Präsentation war erfolgreich. Diese wurde später veröffentlicht.
The presentation was successful. This one was published later.

Demonstrative pronouns (dieser/diese/dieses) se reference zyada saaf aur zyada zor wala ban jaata hai. Yeh khaas kar tab kaam aate hain jab do cheezon mein se ek ki baat karni ho — kyunki er/sie/es se confusion ho sakti hai.
"das" and "dies" often refer to an ENTIRE previous idea or statement, not a single noun.

das aur dies aksar poori pichhli baat ki taraf ishara karte hain, kisi ek noun ki nahi. Isliye yeh badalte bhi nahi — inpar gender ki ending nahi lagti, kyunki inke peeche koi ek noun hi nahi hota.

Verweiswörter are common in conversations, emails, reports, scientific articles, newspapers, presentations, and company communication. Good writers use references instead of repetition.
