The most dangerous mistake is an AMBIGUOUS reference — where the pronoun could point to more than one antecedent. The rest come from wrong gender, wrong number, or a gendered form where an invariable one is needed.
Anna spricht mit Maria. Sie ist freundlich.
Anna spricht mit Maria. Maria ist freundlich.
"Sie" could mean Anna or Maria — both are feminine singular. When two antecedents compete, repeat the name instead.
Der Bericht wurde veröffentlicht. Der Bericht war erfolgreich.
Der Bericht wurde veröffentlicht. Er war erfolgreich.
Once the antecedent is clear, replace the repeated noun with a pronoun — repeating it sounds heavy.
Das Buch ist interessant. Diese ist teuer.
Das Buch ist interessant. Dieses ist teuer.
"Buch" is neuter, so the demonstrative must be "dieses" — not the feminine "diese".
Die Firma investiert in KI. Dieses verbessert die Produktivität.
Die Firma investiert in KI. Dies verbessert die Produktivität.
To point back to a whole idea, use the invariable dies or das — not a gendered form like dieses, which would have to agree with a specific noun.
Die Ergebnisse waren gut. Er waren überzeugend.
Die Ergebnisse waren gut. Sie waren überzeugend.
"Ergebnisse" is plural — the pronoun must be "sie" (plural), not "er" (masculine singular).

Sabse badi galti ambiguous reference hai — jahan pronoun do cheezon mein se kisi ki bhi taraf ishara kar sakta hai. Baaki galtiyan gender ya number galat hone se, ya gendered form wahan lagane se hoti hain jahan dies ya das chahiye tha.
Need to mention something again? Don't automatically repeat the noun — use a Verweiswort if the reference will be clear. If there are two possible antecedents, repeat the noun instead.

Memory trick: every Verweiswort asks "What am I pointing to?" If there is only ONE clear answer, the reference is correct. If there are TWO possibilities, rewrite the sentence. Clarity is more important than avoiding repetition.

Kisi cheez ka dobara zikr karna hai? Noun ko automatically mat dohrao — agar reference saaf hai to Verweiswort use karo. Aur agar do cheezein aisi hain jinki taraf pronoun ishara kar sakta hai, to naam dohraana hi behtar hai. Clarity zyada important hai, repetition se bachna nahi.

The standard B2 paragraph structure: topic sentence → explanation → example → result/conclusion.

German has different moods. Indicative expresses facts. Konjunktiv I is mainly used to report someone else's words objectively. This chapter teaches ONLY the verb forms — the actual use of indirect speech comes in the next chapter.

German mein verb ke alag-alag moods hote hain. Indicative fact batata hai, aur Konjunktiv I tab aata hai jab tum kisi aur ki baat report kar rahe ho. Iska matlab yeh nahi hota ki baat sach hai ya jhooth — yeh sirf signal deta hai ki shabd tumhare nahi, kisi aur ke hain. Isliye news aur reports mein yeh bahut aata hai. Is chapter mein sirf forms banana seekhoge; inka asli use agle chapter mein aayega.
Formula: verb stem + Konjunktiv I endings.

Formula seedha hai: infinitive se -en hatao, aur uspar Konjunktiv I ki ending laga do. Dhyaan do ki ich aur er/sie/es dono -e lete hain — yeh Indicative se ulta lagta hai, isliye yahi sabse zyada confuse karta hai.
Regular verbs (machen, lernen, arbeiten, spielen, kaufen) follow the pattern directly on the stem.

Regular verbs mein stem waise ka waisa rehta hai aur uspar ending lag jaati hai. Dhyaan do ki du machest aur ihr machet Indicative se alag dikhte hain, par ich mache, wir machen aur sie machen bilkul same hain — is baat par neeche wapas aayenge.

Here is the good news: verbs that are irregular in the present tense are NOT irregular in Konjunktiv I. The vowel changes you know from the Indicative (er spricht, er liest, er nimmt, er gibt) disappear completely — you go back to the plain infinitive stem and add the ending.
This is why Konjunktiv I is often the clearest signal that something is reported speech: er spreche can only be Konjunktiv I, because the Indicative would be spricht.

Yahan ek achhi khabar hai — jo verbs present tense mein irregular hain, woh Konjunktiv I mein irregular nahi hote. Indicative wale vowel changes (er spricht, er liest, er nimmt) yahan bilkul gayab ho jaate hain. Tum seedha infinitive ke stem par wapas jaate ho aur ending laga dete ho: er spreche, er lese, er nehme. Isliye yeh forms turant pehchaan mein aa jaati hain — er spreche Indicative ho hi nahi sakta.
Die drei wichtigsten Verben: sein, haben, werden
These three verbs appear constantly in indirect speech — memorize them first.

Yeh teen verbs reported speech mein sabse zyada aate hain, isliye inhe sabse pehle yaad karo. sein sabse important hai kyunki uska stem poora badal jaata hai (sei) aur uski koi bhi form Indicative jaisi nahi hoti.
Modal verbs (dürfen, können, müssen, sollen, wollen, mögen) also form Konjunktiv I with the same endings. Some forms are identical to the Indicative.

Modal verbs bhi wahi endings lete hain. Achhi baat yeh hai ki inka umlaut wapas aa jaata hai — Indicative mein er kann hai, par Konjunktiv I mein er könne. Isliye singular mein yeh forms saaf pehchaan mein aati hain.

There is a clear pattern to this. The er/sie/es form is always distinct, because the Indicative takes -t while Konjunktiv I takes -e. But ich, wir and sie/Sie come out identical to the Indicative for almost every verb — and those are exactly the forms you cannot use as they stand.

That is why er sagt, er komme is unmistakably reported speech, while sie sagen, sie kommen tells the reader nothing. This chapter only flags the problem; the fix (switching to Konjunktiv II) is Chapter 60.
sein is the exception that saves you: sei, seiest, sei, seien, seiet, seien — every single form differs from the Indicative. That is why sei is everywhere in reported speech.

Isme ek saaf pattern hai. er/sie/es ki form hamesha alag dikhti hai, kyunki Indicative mein -t lagta hai aur Konjunktiv I mein -e. Par ich, wir aur sie/Sie lagbhag har verb mein Indicative jaisi hi ho jaati hain — aur wahi forms tum aise use nahi kar sakte. Isliye er komme se turant pata chal jaata hai ki yeh reported speech hai, par sie kommen se kuch pata nahi chalta. Ek verb tumhe bacha leta hai — sein, jiski har form Indicative se alag hai. Isi wajah se reported speech mein sei itna dikhta hai. Iska solution Chapter 60 mein aayega.
These mistakes come from confusing Konjunktiv I with the Indicative, or misapplying the endings.
In reported speech the verb goes into Konjunktiv I, and sein has the irregular stem sei — not the Indicative ist.
The 2nd person singular ending is "-est", not "-e" — "-e" is only for ich and er/sie/es.
The "ihr" form of "sein" in Konjunktiv I is "seiet", following the "-et" ending pattern.
"wir" takes the "-en" ending ("seien"), not "-et" (which belongs to "ihr").
"ich" takes the "-e" ending ("werde"); "-est" belongs to "du" ("du werdest").

Yeh galtiyan do wajah se hoti hain — Indicative ki form hi likh dena, ya endings ko aapas mein badal dena. Ek baat pakki kar lo: -e sirf ich aur er/sie/es ke liye hai, -est sirf du ke liye, aur -et sirf ihr ke liye.

You have two ways to build the reported clause, and both are correct — but they use different word order.
Without dass the clause behaves like a main clause: the verb stays in position 2. With dass it becomes a subordinate clause, so the verb goes to the very end. What you must never do is mix them.
Er sagt, dass er krank sei.
Er sagt, er habe gestern gearbeitet.
Er sagt, dass er gestern gearbeitet habe.
In newspapers and formal reports the version WITHOUT dass is far more common — it sounds lighter and lets several reported sentences follow one another. Use it as your default.

Reported clause banane ke do tareeke hain, aur dono sahi hain — bas word order alag hota hai. dass ke bina clause main clause jaisa chalta hai, isliye verb doosri position par rehta hai: Er sagt, er sei krank. Aur dass lagao to woh subordinate clause ban jaata hai, isliye verb end mein chala jaata hai: Er sagt, dass er krank sei. Galti tab hoti hai jab dono ko mila diya jaata hai. Newspapers aur formal reports mein dass ke bina wala version zyada aata hai, kyunki woh halka lagta hai — isliye ise hi default rakho.

Yeh sabse common badlav hain jo tumhe baar-baar chahiye honge. ist se sei, hat se habe, wird se werde, aur kommt se komme. Inhe pehle pakka kar lo.
These come from leaving the verb in the Indicative, forgetting to shift the pronoun, mismatching the time reference, mixing direct and indirect punctuation, or using dass with main-clause word order.
Reported speech takes Konjunktiv I — sei, not the Indicative ist.
The pronoun shifts to the reporter's perspective. Anna said „ich“, but you are reporting about her — so it becomes sie.
Er berichtet, er sei gestern gekommen.
„gestern“ points to the past, so the reported form must be past too — not the present-tense komme. (Chapter 61 covers this in full.)
Er sagt: „Ich bin krank." / Er sagt, er sei krank.
Pick one. A colon and quotation marks belong to direct speech with the Indicative; a comma and Konjunktiv I belong to indirect speech.
Er sagt, dass er sei krank.
Er sagt, dass er krank sei. / Er sagt, er sei krank.
Both versions are correct German. But dass makes it a subordinate clause, so the verb must go to the END — dass er krank sei. Without dass, normal V2 order applies.

Yeh galtiyan paanch tarah se hoti hain — verb ko Indicative mein chhod dena, pronoun badalna bhool jaana, time reference galat kar dena, direct aur indirect ki punctuation mila dena, ya dass lagane ke baad bhi verb ko doosri position par rakhna.
Quoting exact words? Use direct speech. Reporting someone else's statement? Use Indirekte Rede. Need neutrality? Use Konjunktiv I.
Memory trick: direct speech = exact words, quotation marks. Indirect speech = meaning only, no quotation marks, use Konjunktiv I. Journalists use it to report information without confirming it.

Indirect speech reports NOT when the journalist writes, but when the ORIGINAL speaker meant the event. The original time reference must remain clear — this is different from English, which often collapses everything into the past.

Yahan ek baat samajhna zaroori hai. Tense is baat se tay nahi hota ki report kab likhi jaa rahi hai, balki is baat se ki asli kaam kab hua tha. English mein aksar sab kuch past mein daal diya jaata hai, par German mein original timeline waisi hi rehti hai.
Present stays Present in reported speech.
Agar asli baat present ki thi, to reported speech mein bhi present hi rehta hai — yeh English se alag hai, jahan aksar past ban jaata hai.
Both Perfekt and Präteritum in the original almost always become Konjunktiv I Perfekt in reported speech.
Er sagt, er habe gestern gearbeitet.
Er sagt, er sei früh nach Hause gegangen.
Yeh ek badi aasaani hai — original chahe Perfekt mein ho ya Präteritum mein, reported speech mein dono Konjunktiv I Perfekt ban jaate hain. Matlab past ke liye sirf ek hi form yaad karni hai.

Konjunktiv I Perfekt is built from habe or sei plus the Partizip II — and you pick between them exactly as you already do in the normal Perfekt. Movement and change-of-state verbs take sei; everything else takes habe.
So nothing new has to be learned here: if you know whether a verb takes haben or sein in the Perfekt, you already know whether it takes habe or sei in Konjunktiv I.

Konjunktiv I Perfekt habe ya sei ke saath Partizip II se banta hai — aur in dono mein se kaunsa lagega, yeh bilkul waise hi tay hota hai jaise normal Perfekt mein. Movement aur state change wale verbs sei lete hain (er sei gegangen), aur baaki sab habe (er habe gearbeitet). Matlab yahan naya kuch yaad nahi karna — jo Perfekt mein haben leta hai woh yahan habe lega, aur jo sein leta hai woh sei.
Future stays Future in reported speech.
Er sagt, er werde morgen kommen.
Future bhi waisa hi rehta hai — werden Konjunktiv I mein werde ban jaata hai aur infinitive end mein chala jaata hai: er werde morgen kommen.
Always identify WHEN the action happened — not when it is being reported.

These mistakes come from mismatching the tense with the wrong time reference — the timeline gets confused.
Er sagt, er habe gestern gearbeitet.
„gestern“ signals a past event, so it needs Konjunktiv I Perfekt — not the Präsens form.
Er berichtet, er werde gestern kommen.
Er berichtet, er sei gestern gekommen.
A past event ("gestern") cannot use the Futur form "werde" — use Konjunktiv I Perfekt instead.
Er erklärt, er habe morgen gearbeitet.
Er erklärt, er werde morgen arbeiten.
"morgen" signals a future event — it needs Konjunktiv I Futur I ("werde arbeiten"), not Perfekt.
Er sagt, er komme letzte Woche.
Er sagt, er sei letzte Woche gekommen.
"letzte Woche" is past — the Präsens form "komme" is wrong; use Konjunktiv I Perfekt.
Er berichtet, er sei morgen angekommen.
Er berichtet, er werde morgen ankommen.
"morgen" is future — the Perfekt form "sei angekommen" is wrong; use Konjunktiv I Futur I.

Reporting language communicates what OTHER people say, not what the writer believes. The newspaper reports the statement without confirming it.

Objective reporting avoids personal opinion — never state a claim as your own established fact.

Objective reporting mein apni raay nahi aati. Kisi ki baat ko seedha fact ki tarah mat likho — use us insaan ke naam se attribute karo aur Konjunktiv I use karo. Farak dekho: Der Minister hat recht tumhari raay hai, par Der Minister erklärt, die Lage sei stabil sirf report hai.

These come from doubling the verb, getting the case wrong after a source expression, dropping an article, slipping into your own judgement, or leaving the verb in the Indicative.

Do not add a second verb: sei is already the full Konjunktiv I of sein. (On style: Die Zeitung sagt is not wrong, but berichtet or meldet sounds far more journalistic.)

Written as a plain statement this is your own judgement. In a report you attribute it to the speaker and switch to Konjunktiv I.

Noun + fixed light verb replaces a simple verb for formal register: entscheiden → eine Entscheidung treffen. Never substitute "machen" for the fixed light verb.

Noun + fixed light verb simple verb ki jagah leta hai aur register formal bana deta hai: entscheiden se eine Entscheidung treffen. Har noun ka apna light verb hota hai — Entscheidung ke saath treffen, Antrag ke saath stellen, Diskussion ke saath führen. Har jagah machen lagana sabse aam galti hai.
doch = reminder, contradiction, encouragement. ja = shared knowledge, explanation. eben/halt = calm acceptance ("that's just how it is") — eben more neutral, halt more colloquial.

doch yaad dilata hai ya kisi baat ko kaatta hai, ja batata hai ki baat dono ko pehle se pata hai, aur eben/halt dikhate hain ki baat maan li gayi hai — eben neutral aur halt zyada casual. Chaaron Mittelfeld mein baithte hain, na shuru mein aur na end mein. Aur formal writing mein inme se koi nahi aata.
Verweiswörter (er/sie/es, dieser/diese/dieses, das/dies) avoid repetition but must stay unambiguous. Absatzlogik keeps one idea per paragraph: topic sentence → explanation → example → conclusion.

Verweiswörter repetition se bachate hain, par reference saaf hona chahiye — agar do cheezon mein confusion ho sakti hai to naam dohraana behtar hai. Gender aur number us noun se aate hain jiski baat ho rahi hai, par case naye sentence se. Aur Absatzlogik ka rule ek hi hai: ek paragraph mein ek idea, aur order rehta hai Leitsatz → Erklärung → Beispiel → Schluss.

sein→sei, haben→habe, werden→werde. Present stays Present; Perfekt/Präteritum → Konjunktiv I Perfekt; Future stays Future. Journalistic reporting adds source attribution (laut, nach Angaben von, X zufolge) and never presents opinion as fact.

Timeline waisi hi rehti hai — present present, past ke liye Konjunktiv I Perfekt (habe gearbeitet ya sei gegangen), aur future ke liye werde + infinitive. Dhyaan rakho ki ich, wir aur sie ki forms Indicative jaisi ho jaati hain, isliye wahan Konjunktiv II lagta hai. Aur reporting mein source dena zaroori hai — laut aur zufolge Dativ lete hain.

The article is only half the job. In the Genitiv, masculine and neuter nouns also add -s or -es to the noun itself — this is the part learners most often forget.
Use -es when the noun is one syllable or ends in -s, -ß, -z, -tz: des Kindes, des Gesetzes. Otherwise -s is normal: des Vertrags, des Wetters.

Look closely at every academic example above and you will see the same move: the subject is never a person. Instead of ich, the sentence starts with the study, the data, the results or the analysis — and the verb reports what THEY do.
This one shift does most of the work of sounding academic, because it removes the writer from the sentence without any complicated vocabulary.
Die Daten weisen darauf hin, dass …
The passive and sich lassen (Chapters 44–46) do the same job — they let you report a finding without naming who found it.

These expressions split into two groups, and they behave differently. Some open a dass-clause, so the verb goes to the END. Others fill position 1 themselves, so the verb comes SECOND — before the subject.
Ich bin der Meinung, dass Homeoffice sinnvoll ist.

Meiner Meinung nach sollte man das ändern.
Meines Erachtens ist das zu teuer.
Aus meiner Sicht gibt es bessere Lösungen.
Watch the fixed forms: der Meinung sein keeps its article, and meiner Meinung nach puts nach AFTER the noun. Neither can be shortened.

In expressions ke do group hain aur dono ka word order alag hai. Kuch dass-clause kholte hain, isliye unme verb sentence ke end mein jaata hai: Ich bin der Meinung, dass Homeoffice sinnvoll ist. Aur kuch khud position 1 le lete hain, isliye unke turant baad verb aata hai, subject se pehle: Meiner Meinung nach sollte man das ändern. Do fixed forms dhyaan se yaad rakho — der Meinung sein mein article hamesha rehta hai, aur meiner Meinung nach mein nach noun ke baad aata hai.

Dhyaan rakho ki weil aur da verb ko clause ke end mein bhejte hain, jabki denn, deshalb aur daher ke saath normal order rehta hai. Raay hamesha reason ke saath do — bina reason ke argument adhoora hai.

State the claim first in a dass-clause, then give the reason with weil. Jumping straight to weil leaves the opinion itself unsaid.

A reason has to add NEW information. Repeating the claim in other words explains nothing.

A weil-clause cannot be left hanging — it needs its own subject, its reason and a verb at the end.

Two word-order points carry almost all the mistakes in this chapter.

First: Andererseits, Allerdings, Dennoch and Trotzdem take position 1, so the verb must follow immediately — before the subject. Second: zwar … aber is a fixed pair, and after zwar the verb also comes straight away.

Zwar ist es flexibel, aber es fehlt der Kontakt.
Das Angebot ist zwar teuer, aber es lohnt sich.
jedoch is more flexible — it can open the clause (then verb second) or sit in the middle field: Es ist jedoch teuer.

Is chapter ki zyada-tar galtiyan do word-order points se aati hain. Pehla — Andererseits, Allerdings, Dennoch aur Trotzdem position 1 le lete hain, isliye inke turant baad verb aata hai, subject se pehle: Andererseits ist das teuer. These come from a reason that repeats the claim, forgetting V2 after a fronted connector, breaking a fixed connector pair, misplacing a separable prefix, or stacking two contrast words.
Ich bin dagegen, weil ich dagegen bin.
Ich bin dagegen, weil es zu teuer ist.
A reason has to add NEW information. Repeating your position is not a justification.
Andererseits ich denke, dass es teuer ist.
Andererseits denke ich, dass es teuer ist.
Andererseits fills position 1, so the finite verb has to come second — before the subject.
Zwar ist Homeoffice flexibel, sondern es fehlt der Kontakt.
Zwar ist Homeoffice flexibel, aber es fehlt der Kontakt.
zwar pairs with aber. sondern is only used after a negation, to correct it.
The Dativ object comes early in the clause and the separable prefix zu goes last — nothing follows it.
Trotzdem aber halte ich das für sinnvoll.
Trotzdem halte ich das für sinnvoll.
Two contrastive connectors in a row are redundant — one already carries the contrast.

Yeh galtiyan paanch tarah se hoti hain — reason mein wahi baat dohra dena, fronted connector ke baad verb ko doosri jagah par na rakhna, zwar ke saath galat jodi lagana, separable prefix galat jagah rakhna, ya do contrast words ek saath laga dena.

The phrase itself exists, but mit dir comes BEFORE einverstanden. In a discussion Ich stimme dir zu is the more idiomatic choice.

Before the real exam, check whether you still confuse these classic B2 pairs.
Das Auto ist repariert worden. / Das Auto wurde repariert.
The Perfekt of the Vorgangspassiv takes worden, never geworden — geworden belongs to werden meaning “to become”.
Er sagte, dass er ist müde.
Er sagte, er sei müde. / Er sagte, dass er müde sei.
Two things: reported speech takes Konjunktiv I (sei), and after dass the verb must go to the END.
Das Auto, deren Farbe rot ist.
Das Auto, dessen Farbe rot ist.
The pronoun matches the noun BEFORE the comma. das Auto is neuter, so it takes dessen — deren is for feminine and plural.
Ich stimme dir zu. / Ich bin mit dir einverstanden.
A direct translation of “I agree with you”. German prefers zustimmen + Dativ — and if you do use einverstanden, the phrase comes before it: mit dir einverstanden sein.
Trotzdem das Ergebnis gut war, waren wir nicht zufrieden.
Obwohl das Ergebnis gut war, waren wir nicht zufrieden.
trotzdem is an adverb, so it cannot open a subordinate clause — that job belongs to obwohl. With trotzdem you would write: Das Ergebnis war gut. Trotzdem waren wir nicht zufrieden.

Modalpartikeln like "doch" shift attitude/tone without changing the factual content.

"Trotz" + Genitiv = despite; fits the concessive meaning here.
Which sentence uses the Partizipialattribut correctly?
Partizip II as an attributive adjective: "der [gestern veröffentlichte] Bericht" — modifier before the noun, correctly declined.
Complete: "Sie haben die Aufgabe ___, ohne Fehler zu machen." (Infinitiv mit zu)
"ohne...zu + Infinitiv" is the fixed construction for "without doing something".
Which connector expresses an unexpected contrast (adverb, verb-second)?
"trotzdem" is an adverb triggering verb-second word order; "obwohl"/"weil" are subordinating conjunctions (verb-final).

Open → Ask → Listen → Respond → Clarify → Summarize → Conclude
This seven-part rhythm structures every successful Goethe B2 discussion.

"Es lässt sich feststellen, dass..." removes the personal subject for objective academic style.
Complete the four-step B2 argument structure: Opinion → Reason → ___ → Conclusion.
Opinion + Reason + Example + Conclusion is the core B2 argument model from Chapter 66.
Which sentence correctly forms the bekommen-Passiv?
bekommen-Passiv: bekommen + Partizip II, with the recipient as subject.
What replaces the subject in the "unpersönliches Passiv"?
Nothing — "es" is a placeholder or is dropped
Unpersönliches Passiv has no real grammatical subject; "es" is only a placeholder in first position.
Which sentence uses indirekte Rede (reported speech) correctly at B2?
Sie sagte, sie war krank gewesen.
Reported speech uses Konjunktiv I ("sei") to mark the statement as someone else's claim.
